video.title: Why Your Forehand Sprays, and How to Fix It

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills such as nesting the handle into the V and hitting with an open palm, as well as a self-drop test to calibrate racket face feel.

problem.title_as_question: Why Does Your Forehand Spray, and How Can You Fix It?
problem.definition: The forehand misses inconsistently because a broken sensory link between the hand contours and the racket handle prevents the brain from perceiving momentum and calibrating contact timing.
problem.target_player: Players with sound biomechanics whose forehand sprays due to poor racket face feel or an oversized handle

symptoms.description: The player sprays balls inconsistently and fails to calibrate contact timing across consecutive hits.
The player feels disconnected from the racket handle with no sense of whether the swing is properly loaded or where that load is releasing.
The player struggles or fails to accurately feed or drop-feed balls out of hand using the forehand grip.

causes.statement: The racket handle is too large or wide at the top bevel to fit the contours of the hand, blocking physical nesting.
A broken sensory feedback loop prevents the motor program from receiving enough high-fidelity haptic information to auto-correct timing.
Disengagement and gap creation at the top contact area isolates tactile sensation to the bottom fingers, blinding the player to the swing pressure profile.

angles.summary: Full tactile contact along the upper bevel allows the hand to perceive the racket's momentum and pressure profile during loading and release.
The coach deliberately separates the top of his hand from the grip to show how relying only on the bottom fingers ruins racket face accuracy.
Using an Alcaraz-style grip naturally drives the swing into a larger loop to self-organize racket momentum toward the target.
Spraying the forehand is often diagnosed as faulty swing mechanics when it is actually an un-innervated sensory feedback loop caused by poor handle fit.

solutions.summary: Check whether the top edge of the handle crashes awkwardly into the fingers or whether the hand contours can smoothly caress the bevel.
Nestle the narrow edge of the handle snugly into the V of the hand and hit balls with an open palm to isolate momentum perception to that single haptic contact point.
solutions.external_goal: Direct the ball onto the red target using only top-hand haptic feedback

solutions.summary: Accumulate around a thousand open-palm forehand swings over a month without using the bottom fingers to innervate the top contact area and calibrate the hitting slot.
Test whether you can easily self-drop and feed balls with your forehand grip with the same precision and confidence as with a continental grip.
solutions.external_goal: Drop and feed the ball accurately into a target zone

solutions.summary: Once you can successfully rally with an open palm, re-engage the bottom fingers on the handle while preserving the exact same momentum perception.
